compiled_state.description:
# Populate `RemoteRef` on the inbound path, and correct what it actually protects

## Context / Problem

`RemoteRef` — the backend-neutral identity value `{vendor, instance, remote_id}` defined at
`_backend.py:81` — is **never constructed in production code**. Re-verified against the current
tree, not taken from the original report: in `src/` there is only the frozen dataclass, its
docstring, and one comment in `adapters/jira_datacenter/backend.py:206`. Every construction is in
tests (`backend_support.py:228`, `test_backend_contract.py:96-97`).

Its `instance` field is documented as naming "the concrete deployment (e.g. a Jira site / project
host) so two instances of the same vendor never collide". Nothing populates it, so that sentence
describes an intention rather than a behaviour.

This surfaced in J7 [rebar:b4e3-1de0-3188-40a1], whose AC required asserting "a populated
`RemoteRef.instance`" on a DC-created ticket. That assertion was not satisfiable against any
reconcile pass, so J7's AC was narrowed to the provenance that IS observable (creation_channel +
local-id prefix) and this ticket was filed for the remainder.

## The decision this plan makes

The original draft said "needs design, not just implementation" and left the `instance` source
open. It is decided here, because a plan that defers its central choice cannot be implemented from.

**`instance` is derived from the CONFIGURED base URL** — normalised (scheme dropped, host
lowercased, default port dropped, trailing slash dropped, context path retained, since DC is
commonly served at `/jira`). It is available wherever a backend is constructed
(`JiraDataCenterSettings.url`, `settings.py:45`, itself `reconciler.base_url`), needs no extra REST
round-trip, and requires no operator action.

**The stability objection is real and is answered by SCOPE, not by cleverness.** The draft warned
that "if `instance` is derived from a mutable base URL, an operator moving their instance silently
re-identifies every ticket". That is true of a PERSISTED key. It is not true here for one reason
only, and the reason is sufficient on its own: **this story does not persist a `RemoteRef`
anywhere.** It is an in-memory value returned by a port member. Nothing on disk carries it, so a
URL change re-labels nothing.

A PREVIOUS REVISION ALSO CLAIMED "bindings already key on the issue's immutable numeric id — 7c26
changed exactly that". **That claim was WRONG and is withdrawn**, verified in `binding_store.py`
rather than argued: the binding's primary key is still the Jira KEY (`entry["jira_key"]`, and the
reverse index is `reverse[jira_key]`). 7c26 was ADDITIVE — it added `record_jira_id`/`get_jira_id`
as a supplemental fallback that `note_absent_or_rekey` uses to RE-KEY an entry after a 404. The
argument above never needed that claim, so it is removed rather than repaired.
**This story does NOT make it a persisted key, and says so in BOTH ADRs (0055 and 0035).** Any future story that
persists a `RemoteRef` inherits the stability problem and must solve it there (the candidate is an
operator-set opaque id, or the instance's own server id — neither is needed for in-memory use, and
adding either now would be unused configuration).

## THE CORRECTION THIS TICKET ACTUALLY DELIVERS — the collision claim is FALSE as written

Verified in source rather than reasoned about, and it changes the ticket's conclusion:

* `vendor` ALREADY separates the deployments. Cloud's backend sets `vendor = "jira"`
  (`adapters/jira/backend.py:142`); DC's sets `vendor = "jira-datacenter"`
  (`adapters/jira_datacenter/backend.py:200`). So Cloud-vs-DC never needed `instance`; what
  `instance` disambiguates is TWO DEPLOYMENTS OF THE SAME VENDOR — e.g. two DC instances.
* **Populating `instance` does NOT prevent the collision the docstring claims it prevents.** The
  colliding value is the LOCAL TICKET ID, and `_jira_key_to_local_id`
  (`inbound_translate.py:120-124`) is `"jira-" + jira_key.lower()` — it takes the Jira key and
  NOTHING else. Two DC deployments that each have a project `DIG` both mint `jira-dig-123` for
  their own issue 123, whatever `RemoteRef.instance` says. The field cannot fix that, because
  nothing consults it when the local id is minted.

So AC4 of this ticket ("e369's shared-identity claim is either satisfied or its ADR amended to
match reality") resolves to **AMEND BOTH ADRs** — 0055 and 0035, enumerated in Scope. Making the local id instance-aware would change the
id scheme for every existing Jira-sourced ticket — a breaking, store-wide migration that is not
this ticket and must not be smuggled into it.

## Approach — and THE RECEIVER, which the first revision left unnamed

Round 1 was BLOCKED, correctly and twice, on the same hole: it said "construct a `RemoteRef` on
the inbound path" without naming where the value GOES. With no receiver the construction is a
local variable that is immediately discarded — a no-op that adds a line and changes nothing — and
the "assert on the object the pass actually built" criterion is unsatisfiable by construction,
because nothing exposes it. The correction:

**THE RECEIVER IS A `remote_ref()` MEMBER ON THE `Backend` PORT, and the codebase already told us
so.** The test double has implemented exactly this method since J7 —
`tests/unit/rebar_reconciler/backend_support.py:227-228`:
`def remote_ref(self, remote_id: str) -> RemoteRef: return RemoteRef(vendor=self.vendor,
instance="test", remote_id=remote_id)`. The FAKE satisfies a port member that the PORT never
declared and no real backend implements. That asymmetry is the actual defect underneath this
ticket: the contract tests pass against a fake that is strictly more capable than production.

So:
1. DECLARE `remote_ref(self, remote_id: str) -> RemoteRef` on the `Backend` Protocol.
2. IMPLEMENT it on both concrete backends, returning a `RemoteRef` built from an `instance` value
   the backend was GIVEN AT CONSTRUCTION — not one it resolves when called.
   **`remote_ref()` MUST NOT call `resolve_jira_datacenter_settings()` / `resolve_jira_settings()`
   at call time**, and this is a hard constraint rather than a style preference:
     * `JiraDataCenterBackend.__init__` takes `(transport, client=None)` and receives NO settings,
       so a call-time resolve reaches into ambient config. The contract test constructs backends
       with a `FakeTransport` and no config context, so it would fail for an environment reason
       having nothing to do with what it asserts.
     * this codebase has already been bitten by exactly that shape. A settings-resolving PROPERTY
       earned a `Verified -1` on change cd78: Python 3.12 changed runtime-checkable `Protocol`
       `isinstance` from `hasattr` to `inspect.getattr_static`, so a property that RAISES breaks
       `isinstance` on CI's 3.11 while passing locally on 3.13. The remedy adopted then was to move
       the resolution to the build site, and the same remedy applies here.
   So the backends take the value as a constructor parameter (defaulting to empty), and the
   `build_backend` factories — which already call `resolve_*_settings()` and therefore already hold
   `settings.url` — pass it in. The derivation itself is a small pure helper (the only logic in
   this story).
3. The backend method IS the observable. Assertions read what a real backend returns, which is a
   value that exists in production rather than one a test built.

**NO INVENTED CONSUMER.** Nothing in the pass consumes a `RemoteRef` today, and this story does
NOT wire a call into the inbound path just to have one. Threading a value through a code path that
does not use it would be ceremony that reads as coverage — the reviewer's point restated in the
opposite direction. The deliverable is that the port vocabulary becomes REAL and populated on both
backends; a consumer arrives with the story that needs one.

**THIS CHANGES AN ORIGINAL AC, deliberately, and the reason is recorded.** The ticket as filed said
"a reconcile pass constructs a RemoteRef". Against the current code that is not satisfiable without
adding a consumer that has no purpose, so the criterion is restated as "both real backends return a
populated `RemoteRef` through a declared port member, asserted against the real backend". The
ticket's own text called its scope a "sketch [that] needs design, not just implementation", and its
plan has never been certified, so these are draft criteria being settled rather than settled
criteria being reopened.

## Scope

- `rebar_reconciler/_backend.py` — DECLARE `remote_ref()` on the `Backend` Protocol, and correct
  `RemoteRef`'s docstring. NO change to `RemoteRef`'s FIELDS (it is a frozen value type with a
  passing contract test; changing its shape is out of scope).
- both concrete backends (`adapters/jira/backend.py`, `adapters/jira_datacenter/backend.py`) —
  IMPLEMENT `remote_ref()`, and accept the `instance` value as a CONSTRUCTOR parameter.
- both `build_backend` factories — pass `settings.url` in (they already resolve settings).
- a new pure `instance`-normalisation helper + unit tests.
- the ADRs amended per the section above — BOTH files that carry the claim, named rather than
  gestured at: `docs/adr/0055-jira-family-sub-seam.md` (its ":146" line calls `RemoteRef.instance`
  "INTENDED design, not an existing mechanism", and its ":317" open-issue entry says it "remains
  unbuilt", citing this ticket) and `docs/adr/0035-reconciler-vendor-adapter-seam.md`, which
  introduces `RemoteRef`. Amending only one leaves the other asserting the opposite.

**NOT in scope:** wiring a `remote_ref()` call into the inbound path or any other pass (no consumer
exists; see Approach); changing `_jira_key_to_local_id` or the local-id scheme (a breaking
store-wide migration); persisting `RemoteRef` anywhere; any new config key.

## Testing

* the normalisation helper is unit-tested directly: two DIFFERENT deployment URLs give DIFFERENT
  `instance` values, and two spellings of the SAME deployment (trailing slash, upper-case host,
  explicit default port) give the SAME one. The second half is the one that matters — a helper that
  merely returns the URL passes the first half trivially.
* BOTH REAL BACKENDS return a `RemoteRef` with a non-empty `instance` from `remote_ref()`,
  asserted against a real backend object rather than the fake — the fake has implemented this
  method all along, so a test that only exercises the fake would pass today, before any change.
* the contract test constructs those backends with NO ambient config, passing the `instance`
  EXPLICITLY, and still passes — which is what proves `remote_ref()` reads constructor state
  rather than resolving settings at call time. If it needs a config fixture, the constraint above
  has been violated. A second construction WITHOUT the argument must return the empty default,
  distinguishing "used what it was given" from "found a value elsewhere".
* two backends configured at different base URLs produce `RemoteRef`s that are NOT equal, and two
  configured at the same URL produce equal ones (`RemoteRef` is frozen and value-equal, which
  `test_backend_contract.py:96-97` already pins).
* a REGRESSION GUARD for the correction above: a test asserting that two deployments sharing a
  project key DO still mint the same local id, with a docstring naming this as known and bounded.
  Pinning the limitation stops a later reader assuming `instance` solved it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] a pure helper derives `instance` from a base URL; different deployments differ, and
      equivalent spellings of one deployment (trailing slash / case / default port) agree
- [ ] `Backend` DECLARES `remote_ref()`, both concrete backends IMPLEMENT it, and each returns a
      `RemoteRef` whose `vendor` and `remote_id` are correct and whose `instance` is EXACTLY THE
      VALUE THE CONSTRUCTOR WAS GIVEN — asserted against the REAL backends, constructed in the test
      with an EXPLICIT instance argument and no ambient config. There is no tension between "no
      config" and "non-empty instance": the value is non-empty BECAUSE the test passes one in, and
      that is precisely what proves `remote_ref()` reads its constructor state rather than
      resolving settings. A backend constructed WITHOUT the argument returns the empty default,
      which is also asserted — so the test distinguishes "took the injected value" from "found one
      somewhere else". (This restates the ticket's original "a reconcile pass constructs a
      RemoteRef": nothing consumes one, so satisfying that literally would mean adding a
      purposeless consumer. Reasoning in Approach.)
- [ ] two backends at different base URLs yield unequal `RemoteRef`s for the same `remote_id`
- [ ] the chosen `instance` source is documented, INCLUDING what happens when the base URL changes,
      and including that this story does not persist a `RemoteRef` anywhere — which is the whole
      reason a URL change re-labels nothing on disk
- [ ] BOTH ADRs named in Scope (0055 and 0035) and `RemoteRef`'s docstring are AMENDED to state
      that `instance` does NOT prevent
      local-id collision between two same-vendor deployments — `_jira_key_to_local_id` derives the
      id from the Jira key alone — and that `vendor` already separates Cloud from DC
- [ ] a test pins that known limitation, so it cannot be silently assumed fixed
- [ ] no new operator-facing config key is introduced, `_jira_key_to_local_id` is unchanged, and no
      `remote_ref()` call is added to any pass (the port member is the deliverable; a consumer is not)
- [ ] `remote_ref()` resolves NO configuration when called — the `instance` value arrives via the
      constructor from the `build_backend` factory, and the contract test constructs both real
      backends with no config context to prove it
- [ ] the contract test covers `remote_ref()` for the REAL backends, closing the gap where
      `backend_support.FakeBackend` implemented a port member production did not
compiled_state.title: Populate RemoteRef on the inbound path so deployment identity is observable
